public_rationale: On July 3, 2026, TrendForce reported that suppliers' prioritization of AI applications kept LPDRAM supply tight and supported price increases [e1]. Its March 31 report forecast a 70–75% quarter-on-quarter rise in NAND contract prices for Q2 2026; it did not measure realized Q2 prices [e2]. On July 5, The Buildout attributed a roughly $100 billion estimate for a one-gigawatt Nvidia-based data center to Jensen Huang [e3]. These items do not establish a comparable rise from $50 billion to $100 billion in less than ten months or quantify how much RAM and storage inflation contributed [e1, e2, e3].
limitations: No matched pair of cost estimates establishes the doubling within September 7, 2025–July 7, 2026.
Power definitions, hardware specifications and included project costs are not reconciled.
No cost breakdown attributes the claimed increase to memory and storage inflation.
The evidence does not establish price increases across all electronics.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI data center demand has inflated RAM and storage costs, doubling the cost of a gigawatt data center from $50B to $100B in under 10 months.

statement.excerpt: A semiconductor bubble, where supply chains have become saturated with demand from those building AI data centers, inflating the cost of RAM and storage, making all electronics more expensive, including those inside the AI data centers, creating a vicious cycle that has doubled the cost of a gigawatt data center from $50 billion to $100 billion in a little under 10 months.

from_speaker: demand from those building AI data centers
inflating the cost of RAM and storage
doubled the cost of a gigawatt data center
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that comparable, fully equipped AI data centers became roughly twice as expensive per gigawatt, with AI-driven memory and storage inflation materially causing that increase.
Use the ten months ending on the post date as the outer observation window. The two comparable estimates must themselves be less than ten months apart.
A change in equipment generation, computing capacity per gigawatt, or included construction costs cannot automatically be treated as price inflation.
No accounting or project-cost basis is specified.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable dated budgets or cost estimates establish an increase from approximately USD 50 billion to USD 100 billion per gigawatt in less than ten months, and component-price evidence attributes a material part of that increase to AI-driven RAM and storage shortages.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable cost records show that the claimed doubling did not occur, or a reliable cost decomposition shows that the increase came from changed specifications or other causes rather than the stated memory-and-storage mechanism.

evidence.explanation: Supports the proposed memory-supply mechanism. It does not establish a doubling of comparable data-center costs.
Shows substantial expected storage-price pressure. This is a forecast issued in March, not proof of realized second-quarter prices or whole-project costs.
Corroborates circulation of the upper estimate. The summary does not establish the original statement's exact date, consistent specifications, or the reason for any increase.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Comparable dated budgets or cost estimates less than ten months apart within the specified window, plus realized component prices and a cost breakdown separating AI-driven RAM and storage inflation from changes in hardware, construction scope and other costs.
